strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: hallucination of library dependencies in LLM-based statement autoformalization, with a clear illustrative failure case (Figure 1a).
The generation-plus-verification paradigm (DDR) is a sensible departure from embedding-based retrieval, avoiding the need for a pre-specified top-k and sidestepping encoder training issues.

The suffix-array verification mechanism is algorithmically sound, with correct complexity analysis (O(N) construction, O(log N) query), and is shown to meaningfully speed up large-scale dependency extraction (2.5 days -> under 2 hours), enabling construction of a 500k-sample dataset.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental design: retrieval-only comparisons (Table 2) as well as downstream autoformalization comparisons (Table 3) across multiple difficulty bins, several strong ICL baselines (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen2.5-Max), and multi-attempt reliability/efficiency analyses (Figures 4-5).
Uses an established, human-aligned semantic equivalence metric (BEq) from prior work rather than relying solely on weaker surface metrics.
Dataset and methodology are stated to be open-sourced and are described as generalizable to other formal corpora/provers, which if realized would benefit the community.
weaknesses: A major confound: the DDR model is built on Qwen3-32B while the RA/R@k baselines are built on the much smaller InternLM2-Math-Base-7B. Because the comparison changes both the retrieval method and the base model simultaneously, it is impossible to attribute the reported gains cleanly to the DDR method itself rather than to base-model capacity; a controlled ablation with matched base models for DDR vs. R@k is needed.

The R@5/R@10 embedding baseline achieves suspiciously low precision/recall (e.g., 0.02-0.13), which is far weaker than typically reported for dense retrieval systems in this space; the paper does not sufficiently investigate or justify why the baseline is this weak (e.g., embedding model choice, indexing granularity), leaving open whether the baseline is a fair, well-tuned point of comparison.

Test sets are small (200 samples per difficulty bin, 5 bins total = 1000 test items) and no variance/significance testing is reported for Table 3 differences, despite the paper itself emphasizing multi-attempt stability elsewhere; some reported gains (e.g., Diff45 BEq 0.59 vs 0.54) are numerically modest and could plausibly fall within noise.

Method and dataset construction are validated only on Lean4/Mathlib via FineLeanCorpus; claims about generalizability to "other formal corpora" and other theorem provers (Coq, Isabelle) are asserted but not empirically tested.

The paper omits comparison to more recent/relevant dependency-retrieval work referenced in its own related work section (e.g., ARIA, Wang et al. 2025b), which limits the completeness of the empirical positioning against the current state of the art.

Some presentation/reproducibility gaps: the open-source dataset link is blank in the manuscript, one in-text citation is empty/missing (page 2, "identifiers and construction of syntax ()"), and the DDR hallucination/failure rate after verification is not explicitly quantified in the main text.

The paper's own Discussion section acknowledges DDR loses compatibility with full retrieval metadata (documentation, usage) required by the baseline autoformalizer framework, and metadata fields were simply set to None for baselines during evaluation — this ad hoc handling could bias the downstream comparison in Table 3 in DDR's favor since the baseline's expected information pipeline is degraded.
Minor writing/grammar issues throughout (e.g., "three direction," "Similiar," "an highly efficient method," "tositives") suggest the manuscript would benefit from a careful proofreading pass.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem in autoformalization: hallucination of formal identifiers and the poor precision/recall of embedding-based dependency retrieval when a formal library grows to hundreds of thousands of entries.

The suffix-array-based verification mechanism is efficient and clearly analyzed (O(N) construction, O(log N) verification), providing a plausible engineering path to scaling dataset construction (500K+ samples extracted from FineLeanCorpus in under 2 hours vs. 2.5 days).

The paper evaluates across multiple difficulty tiers and includes both retrieval-only and downstream autoformalization metrics (precision/recall/F1, TypeC, BEq), plus multi-attempt reliability/efficiency analyses (Figures 4-5), which is a reasonably thorough evaluation protocol for the claims being made.
Releasing a large dependency-retrieval dataset, if it materializes, could be a useful resource for follow-up work in this niche.
Honest discussion of a genuine limitation (DDR cannot retrieve full item metadata due to name-disambiguation issues) in Section 5.
weaknesses: The magnitude of the reported retrieval gains is implausible and undermines confidence in the central empirical claim: R@5/R@10 baseline precision is only 0.02-0.13 while DDR reaches 0.85-0.93 (Table 2), an order-of-magnitude gap for a baseline drawn from a recent, peer-reviewed ICLR paper (Liu et al., 2025b). No analysis is given of why this baseline performs so poorly, whether it was reproduced faithfully, whether the evaluation protocol (suffix-based matching) is symmetric between the generative DDR outputs and the selection-based baseline outputs, or whether hyperparameters for the baseline were tuned at all. This large, unexplained discrepancy is a serious soundness concern rather than simply an exciting result.

The downstream autoformalization gains in Table 3 are far more modest (often 2-5 points in BEq) than the retrieval gains in Table 2 would predict, and this inconsistency is not analyzed or reconciled; it raises the question of whether the retrieval metric is measuring something disconnected from what actually helps the downstream task.

Core technical novelty is limited: using an LLM to directly generate library dependency names and then checking existence via string matching (suffix array/binary search) is a natural and largely engineering-level idea; the suffix array mechanism itself is a standard, off-the-shelf data structure with no algorithmic contribution beyond applying it to this setting.

No ablation isolating the contribution of the generation-plus-verification paradigm from simply using a larger/better fine-tuned model; it is unclear how much of DDR's advantage stems from SFT on 500K in-domain examples (which itself risks memorizing likely dependencies for similar-looking problems) versus the proposed method's structural design.

Insufficient detail on DDR inference: how many candidate dependencies are generated, how failures/verification rejections are handled, and what fraction of generated items fail the suffix-array check are not reported, limiting reproducibility of the core retrieval pipeline.

Train/test split is based on a difficulty attribute rather than de-duplication of near-identical problems; given FineLeanCorpus's likely templated math-word-problem style (as shown in Appendix A examples), this raises unaddressed contamination/leakage concerns that could inflate reported DDR performance.

No human evaluation, qualitative error analysis, or discussion of failure modes for DDR (e.g., cases where generated dependencies exist in the library but are semantically irrelevant, which the suffix-array check cannot filter).

Presentation issues: multiple typos ("Similiar," "tositives"), Figure 4 caption mislabels a series as "RAW," and some baseline notation ("topological-informalization retrieval") is unclear/unexplained relative to the cited paper's actual method name.

The claimed scalability/online-deployment benefit is asserted but never measured empirically (e.g., no latency comparison between DDR's LLM-generation-based inference and embedding-based retrieval, despite this being highlighted as a key motivation).

strengths: The core idea—replacing select-then-verify embedding retrieval with a generate-then-verify (DDR) paradigm—is simple, well-motivated, and directly addresses documented failure modes (hallucinated identifiers, poor precision/recall of embedding retrieval) in prior autoformalization RAG pipelines.

The suffix-array verification mechanism is a clean engineering contribution with clear complexity analysis (O(N) construction, O(log N) query), and its practical payoff (reducing dependency extraction from ~2.5 days to <2 hours on 500k+ samples) is a concrete, useful efficiency gain for dataset construction and potential online deployment.

The paper contributes and plans to open-source a large (500k+) dependency-annotated dataset built from FineLeanCorpus, which could be broadly useful to the community for training future retrieval/autoformalization models.

Experiments span multiple difficulty levels and a reasonably broad set of baselines (several strong general LLMs via ICL, an SFT baseline, and embedding-based R@5/R@10 retrieval), and include secondary analyses of multi-attempt consistency and generation efficiency (Figures 4-5) beyond single-shot accuracy.
The paper is candid about a genuine limitation of DDR (loss of full metadata for generated dependency names due to short/unqualified names), which strengthens the credibility of its claims.
weaknesses: The R@5/R@10 baseline numbers in Table 2 (precision/recall in the 0.02-0.19 range) seem implausibly weak for a published SOTA method (Liu et al., 2025b); no analysis is given for why the baseline underperforms so drastically, raising concern about whether it was faithfully reproduced/tuned, which undermines the magnitude of the reported DDR improvement.

The suffix-based matching used to compute precision/recall for DDR could itself introduce false positives when a short/unqualified generated name coincidentally matches an unrelated library object with the same suffix (e.g., Nat.sqrt vs Real.sqrt, explicitly acknowledged as a real ambiguity problem in Section 3.1) — it is unclear how this ambiguity was resolved or bounded in the reported metrics, which affects trust in the headline precision/recall numbers.

Comparisons across Table 3 conflate multiple confounds: RA/RA+DDR are built on a much smaller base model (InternLM2-Math-Base-7B + Qwen3-32B for retrieval) while ICL baselines use very different, much larger general-purpose LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1); attributing the performance gap primarily to the retrieval method versus base-model capability/training data differences is not cleanly disentangled.

The Discussion section notes that DDR's outputs are incompatible with the full RA+R@k framework (missing name/usage/documentation metadata, all set to None at inference), meaning the RA+DDR and RA+R@k comparisons are not run under equivalent information conditions — this could bias the comparison in either direction and is not quantitatively controlled for.

No significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the relatively small test sets (200 samples per difficulty bucket, single retrieval pass per Table 2), making it hard to assess whether observed differences (e.g., in Table 3 BEq scores) are robust rather than sampling noise.
The dataset release link is left as an empty placeholder in the manuscript, which is a reproducibility concern for the current submission version.

The method and dataset construction are validated on a single formal library (Lean 4 Mathlib) via a single source corpus (FineLeanCorpus); the claimed generalizability of the suffix-array/DDR methodology to other formal corpora and provers is asserted but not empirically demonstrated.

There is no direct error analysis of DDR failures (e.g., what fraction of generated dependency names fail SA verification and are dropped, and how this specifically affects recall at higher difficulty levels where recall visibly degrades from ~0.74 to ~0.46 in Table 2).

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem (hallucination in formal dependency retrieval for autoformalization) with a simple, efficient generate-then-verify paradigm.

The Suffix Array Check (SAC) mechanism has favorable theoretical complexity (O(sM log N)) and is reused effectively for three purposes: dataset construction, inference-time verification, and downstream analyses (hallucination quantification, difficulty estimation).

Comprehensive experiments spanning five ICL LLMs (Claude, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4o, Ling-flash, Qwen-Max) and an SFT baseline (RA), across five difficulty-stratified test sets, showing consistent improvements in both retrieval precision/recall and downstream autoformalization metrics (TypeC, BEq).
Useful quantitative framing of ICL hallucination rates (Table 2), which is a novel and interesting analysis not previously reported in this explicit form.

Large-scale (500k+) dependency retrieval dataset construction methodology is described as generalizable to other formal corpora, and the training/inference pipeline (SFT + SAC filtering) is reasonably reproducible given the appendix details on hyperparameters and prompts.
weaknesses: The dataset release link is left blank in the text ("has been made open-access at" with no URL), undermining a central reproducibility claim.

The core technical novelty is modest: SAC is essentially an application of known suffix-array/n-gram matching techniques (cited from Liu et al. 2024) to a lookup task, and DDR is a fairly direct SFT-based generate-then-filter approach; the conceptual contribution is more engineering integration than a new method.

The evaluation protocol for retrieval precision/recall uses a lenient substring/sublist matching criterion (Appendix C) between generated and ground-truth identifiers, which could differentially favor DDR's abbreviated outputs and makes the large precision/recall gap over baselines harder to interpret at face value.

The R@5/R@10 baseline (Liu et al. 2025b) precision figures reported here (0.02-0.10) seem unusually low relative to what one would expect from an embedding-based retriever, raising questions about whether the baseline was faithfully reproduced/tuned, which affects the fairness of the primary comparison.

The RA+DDR integration explicitly suffers from a "format mismatch" with the prior RA framework (abbreviated names vs. full metadata), acknowledged in Limitations, which weakens the claim that DDR is a fully plug-and-play, generalizable module.
No experiments beyond Lean4/Mathlib despite claims of general applicability to other formal corpora (Coq, Isabelle); the generalization claim is untested.

The proposed Depend Rate/Depend Length difficulty metrics are only qualitatively compared against LLM-assigned difficulty labels for a handful of difficulty bins, without a rigorous validation against human judgments or ground truth.
Writing quality has minor grammatical issues and some presentation gaps (e.g., truncated corpus citation list, awkward phrasing) that slightly reduce clarity.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem in autoformalization: hallucination of nonexistent library dependencies, which directly undermines downstream formal verification pipelines.

The generation-plus-verification paradigm (DDR + SAC) is a sensible engineering idea, and the suffix-array-based existence check is efficient and scalable compared to brute-force string matching or embedding-based retrieval.

Fairly broad empirical coverage: experiments span multiple difficulty levels, several proprietary and open LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-Max, Ling-flash), and both SFT (RA) and ICL autoformalization pipelines.
Explicit quantification of hallucination rates in dependency generation is a useful diagnostic contribution that prior work lacked.
Construction and intended release of a large (500k+) dependency-retrieval dataset could be a useful community resource if properly released.
The proposed Depend Rate/Depend Length metrics offer an interesting, non-LLM-based lens on formalization difficulty, complementing subjective LLM-graded difficulty labels.
weaknesses: Confounded comparison: DDR is fine-tuned on Qwen3-32B, while the RA baseline it is combined with/compared against uses InternLM2-Math-Base-7B; the large difference in base model scale is not controlled for, so improvements attributed to the DDR method could instead (partly) reflect the stronger base model, undermining the central empirical claims.

The precision/recall evaluation relies on a lenient, custom suffix/sublist substring-matching criterion to reconcile DDR's abbreviated outputs with fully-qualified ground-truth identifiers; this heuristic is not validated against manual judgment and could systematically favor DDR's short-name outputs over baselines that output full identifiers, inflating DDR's reported precision/recall advantage.

Downstream autoformalization gains from DDR are inconsistent: in several settings (e.g., Qwen-Max Diff45 TypeC, Ling-flash Diff01 TypeC) DDR performs on par with or worse than the no-retrieval baseline, weakening the 'plug-and-play, consistently superior' claim made in the text.

Reproducibility is compromised: the dataset release URL is missing/blank in the manuscript ('has been made open-access at' with no link), and several implementation details (e.g., exact prompts for some steps, validation of SAC-derived training labels) are only partially specified.

The training-data construction via SAC (extracting identifiers used in existing formal code as 'dependencies') is not validated for label quality — code may reference incidental or boilerplate identifiers unrelated to the true conceptual dependencies, and no manual audit of label precision is reported.

The 'formalization difficulty' analysis via Depend Rate/Length is based on only four aggregated subset averages, which is a very small and potentially circular evidentiary base (the metric is derived from the same DDR/SAC pipeline being validated) to support claims of it being a 'sound mechanism' superseding LLM-based difficulty grading.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting despite relatively small per-condition test sets (200 statements) and stochastic pass@8 sampling, making it hard to assess whether reported differences are robust.
Missing comparison against other recent, directly relevant retrieval-augmented autoformalization systems mentioned in related work (e.g., ARIA), limiting the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' claim.

Overall writing quality has multiple grammatical errors and unclear/truncated sentences, suggesting the submission was not fully polished, which affects clarity and gives an impression of insufficient care in preparation.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: hallucination of formal dependencies in statement autoformalization, with a clear articulation of why existing embedding/select-based retrieval methods are inadequate.

The generate-then-verify paradigm (DDR + SAC) is a sensible and simple design, avoiding the need to train/maintain an encoder over a huge and growing library, and the suffix-array verification is an efficient, principled solution (O(sM log N)) with clear algorithmic description (Figure 2).

Large, open-sourced dataset (500K+ samples) constructed via a scalable SAC-based pipeline from FineLeanCorpus; the construction methodology is described as generalizable to other formal corpora, which could benefit the community.

Comprehensive experimental coverage: retrieval precision/recall (Table 3), hallucination quantification (Table 2), and downstream autoformalization performance under both SFT (Table 4) and ICL settings across five difficulty bins and multiple LLMs (Table 5), plus pass@k consistency/efficiency analyses (Figures 3-6).

Reported gains are large and mostly consistent: DDR nearly eliminates hallucination (<2%) versus ~30% for ICL baselines, and yields sizeable precision/recall improvements over R@5/R@10 and prompt-based retrieval, translating into consistent (if sometimes modest) BEq gains downstream.

Reasonably transparent limitations section (DDR's incompatibility with full-metadata retrieval frameworks, special-case constructs like MOD, library versioning issues) and detailed appendix with hyperparameters and prompts supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The precision/recall evaluation protocol (Appendix C) uses a fairly permissive substring/sublist suffix-matching criterion to count true positives for DDR's abbreviated dependency names; since DDR's outputs are by construction short/abbreviated, this could inflate its apparent precision relative to baselines evaluated on full qualified names, raising fairness concerns about the headline retrieval comparison in Table 3.

The chosen selection-based baselines (R@5/R@10 from Liu et al. 2025b) perform extremely poorly (precision 0.02-0.10), which is a suspiciously large gap versus DDR (0.82-0.92); it is unclear whether this reflects a genuinely weak SOTA method or an unfavorable/under-tuned baseline implementation, weakening the claim of 'significantly outperforming SOTA'.

The claim that SAC/Depend Rate and Depend Length provide a 'sound mechanism' for assessing formalization difficulty is supported only by a coarse ranking-correlation argument over four combined difficulty bins (Section 4.1), which is weak statistical evidence for what is presented as a notable contribution (listed as contribution #4).

DDR is trained and evaluated entirely within the FineLeanCorpus/Mathlib ecosystem; no experiments test generalization to a different formal library or theorem prover, despite claims that the dataset-construction methodology is broadly generalizable.

The combination of RA and DDR is described as suffering from a 'format mismatch' (abbreviated vs. full dependency names), yet results are still reported without full clarity on how this mismatch was resolved in practice, leaving some ambiguity about the validity of the RA+DDR numbers in Table 4.

Minor presentation/reproducibility issues: the dataset release link is blank in the text (page 5), some grammatical errors, and the paper reports only filtered (post-hallucination-removal) precision/recall separately from hallucination rates rather than a single combined metric that would give a more complete picture of raw retrieval quality.
